themes.label: Foundations
themes.note: What monopoly is, what it costs and how to measure it.

themes.label: Pricing
themes.note: Price discrimination, bundling, durable goods and commitment.

themes.label: Collusion & entry
themes.note: Cartels, price wars, deterrence and where firms locate.

themes.label: Exclusion & platforms
themes.note: Tying, foreclosure, raising rivals' costs and two-sided markets.

themes.label: Measuring market power
themes.note: Structural estimates of markups in real industries.

themes.label: Regulation
themes.note: Utilities, procurement, licensing and incentive contracts.

themes.label: Macro & money
themes.note: Markups, concentration, sticky prices and monetary policy.

items.title: One More Seller
items.dek: In 1838, Augustin Cournot worked out how far a price should fall each time another seller joins a market. I asked whether America's generic drug market follows his rule.
items.finding: The first generic takes off about 30%, close to Cournot's prediction

figures.alt: Generic price by number of sellers
Within-product price by number of sellers

items.paper: Cournot, A. A. (1838). Recherches sur les principes mathématiques de la théorie des richesses. Paris: L. Hachette. English translation by N. T. Bacon, Researches into the Mathematical Principles of the Theory of Wealth, New York and London: Macmillan, 1897.

items.title: What the Traffic Will Bear
items.dek: In 1920, Arthur Pigou sorted price discrimination into three degrees and said railways charge valuable goods more than cheap ones. A century later, I checked what American railroads actually charge.
items.finding: Valuable goods do not carry the markups Pigou predicted

figures.alt: Rail markups against the value of the goods
Revenue by R/VC zone within each commodity

items.paper: A. C. Pigou, The Economics of Welfare, London: Macmillan, 1920. Part II, chapter XIV, "Discriminating Monopoly" (pp. 240–255); chapter XV, "The Special Problem of Railway Rates" (pp. 256–282); Appendix III, § 24 (pp. 951–952). Chapters XVII and XVIII in the fourth edition (1932).

items.title: Short of Orders
items.dek: In 1926, Piero Sraffa argued that what holds a business back is its customers, not its costs. A century later, I asked American factories again.
items.finding: Three in four factories running below capacity are short of orders

figures.alt: Why US factories produced less than they could, 2013-2026
Unit cost by plant size

items.paper: Piero Sraffa, "The Laws of Returns under Competitive Conditions," Economic Journal 36(144), December 1926, pp. 535–550. A first footnote states that the opening pages summarize the conclusions of the author's Italian paper "Relazioni fra costo e quantità prodotta," Annali di Economia, Vol. II.

items.title: The Price of a Stamp
items.dek: In 1927, Frank Ramsey worked out how to raise a fixed sum with the least harm, by charging most where buyers have the fewest ways out. I checked whether the Postal Service's 2025 prices follow his rule.
items.finding: Postal markups do not follow Ramsey's rule

figures.alt: Markup against inverse elasticity
Ramsey price changes by product

items.paper: F. P. Ramsey, "A Contribution to the Theory of Taxation," The Economic Journal 37(145), March 1927, pp. 47–61. Read alongside its usual companion, M. Boiteux, "Sur la gestion des monopoles publics astreints à l'équilibre budgétaire," Econometrica 24(1), 1956, pp. 22–40.

items.title: Next Door to the Competition
items.dek: In 1929 Harold Hotelling argued that rival sellers crowd together and that distance gives each of them a little monopoly. I asked again with 174,674 American stores.
items.finding: Small stores sit beside their rivals

figures.alt: Co-location of rival chains relative to chance
Party medians in Congress

items.paper: Harold Hotelling, "Stability in Competition," Economic Journal 39(153), March 1929, pp. 41–57.

items.title: A Restaurant on Every Corner
items.dek: In 1933, Edward Chamberlin explained how a market crowded with small sellers can charge more than cost and still earn nothing extra. Ninety-three years later, I checked his answer against the tax returns of American business.
items.finding: Restaurants, salons and garages have pricing power and almost nothing left over

figures.alt: Margin over variable cost and economic profit by industry
Establishment size and city size, by trade

items.paper: Edward Hastings Chamberlin, The Theory of Monopolistic Competition: A Re-orientation of the Theory of Value, Harvard Economic Studies vol. 38, Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1933. The copyright page of the 1948 sixth edition lists the years 1933, 1937, 1938, 1942, 1946 and 1948.

items.title: Who Pays Full Price
items.dek: In 1933, Joan Robinson worked out when a seller can charge rich and poor buyers different prices for the same thing. Nine decades later, I tested her theory on what American colleges charge.
items.finding: The most selective colleges charge the widest price gaps

figures.alt: Income discount against admission rate
Pell share against income discount

items.paper: Joan Robinson, The Economics of Imperfect Competition, London, Macmillan, 1933. The review covers Book V, chapter 15 ("Price Discrimination," pp. 179–202) and chapter 16 ("The Moral of Price Discrimination," pp. 203–208), with the two formulas from Book I, chapter 2 (p. 36) and Book II, chapter 3 (p. 64) on which they rest.

items.title: The Price-Cost Gap
items.dek: In 1934, Abba Lerner proposed measuring monopoly power by how far a price sits above the cost of one more unit, and said that this gap is not the same thing as profit. I measured it across American industry in 2025 and followed where the money goes.
items.finding: A wide gap is common, and most of it is spent

figures.alt: Lerner index against operating margin, 83 US industries
Lerner index over time, BEA and public companies

items.paper: Lerner, A. P. (1934). "The Concept of Monopoly and the Measurement of Monopoly Power." Review of Economic Studies 1(3): 157–175 (issue dated June 1934). doi:10.2307/2967480.

items.title: The Best and Worst Factories in America
items.dek: In 1935, John Hicks suggested that companies with no one to fear stop trying so hard. Ninety years later, I looked inside American manufacturing to see whether he was right.
items.finding: Concentrated industries carry a wider spread in output per hour

figures.alt: Productivity spread against concentration, 2017
Change in concentration against change in TFP spread

items.paper: Hicks, J. R. (1935). "Annual Survey of Economic Theory: The Theory of Monopoly." Econometrica 3(1), January 1935, pp. 1–20. Author's affiliation as printed at the end of the article: London School of Economics.

items.title: The Perennial Gale
items.dek: In 1942, Joseph Schumpeter argued that big companies with market power, not crowds of small competitors, are what make things cheaper over time. I asked the same question of 471 American manufacturing industries.
items.finding: Concentrated industries raised productivity faster

figures.alt: TFP growth by concentration quintile
Price in hours of labor against concentration
Concentration in 2002 and 2022

items.paper: Joseph A. Schumpeter, Capitalism, Socialism and Democracy. New York: Harper & Brothers, 1942. Chapters 7 ("The Process of Creative Destruction") and 8 ("Monopolistic Practices"), with chapter 5 ("The Rate of Increase of Total Output") for the growth figures the argument builds on.

items.title: Who Makes Everything?
items.dek: In 1951, Joe Bain asked whether the companies that dominate American industry get rich doing it. Seventy-five years later, I asked again.
items.finding: Concentrated industries no longer earn more

figures.alt: Markups in US manufacturing, 2013–2025
Concentration changes vs. profit changes

items.title: Room for One More Plant
items.dek: In 1958, Franco Modigliani worked out how the size of an efficient factory could let established firms charge more than cost without inviting new competitors. I asked whether that still shows up in American manufacturing.
items.finding: Big plants go with concentrated industries

figures.alt: Scale barrier and price-cost margin, 2022
Within-industry changes, 2017 to 2022

items.paper: Franco Modigliani, "New Developments on the Oligopoly Front," Journal of Political Economy 66(3), June 1958, pp. 215–232.

items.title: Scrubbers, Shutdowns and the Rate Base
items.dek: In 1962, Harvey Averch and Leland Johnson argued that a utility paid a fixed return on its capital will build too much of it. I asked again, using the American coal fleet and thirty years of utility books.
items.finding: Regulated utilities spent twice as much capital per kilowatt

figures.alt: New control capital and coal exits by ownership group
Earned return on equity vs. market yields

items.paper: Harvey Averch and Leland L. Johnson, "Behavior of the Firm Under Regulatory Constraint," American Economic Review 52(5), December 1962, pp. 1052–1069. Circulated as RAND Corporation paper P-2488-1, "Behavior of the Firm Subject to External Regulatory Constraint."

items.title: The Profit You Already Have
items.dek: In 1962, Kenneth Arrow argued that a protected monopolist has less reason to invent than a competitive industry, because every improvement replaces profit it already earns. I asked whether American manufacturing looks that way today.
items.finding: Concentrated industries do not spend less on research

figures.alt: R&D intensity against four-firm concentration, 2017 and 2022
Changes in concentration and R&D intensity, 2017 to 2022

items.paper: Kenneth J. Arrow, "Economic Welfare and the Allocation of Resources for Invention," in Universities-National Bureau Committee for Economic Research, The Rate and Direction of Inventive Activity: Economic and Social Factors, Princeton University Press for the National Bureau of Economic Research, 1962, pp. 609–626 (with a comment by C. J. Hitch, pp. 625–626).

items.title: The Secret Price Cut
items.dek: In 1964, George Stigler argued that a few sellers can hold prices up only as long as they can catch the one who quietly undercuts. I asked again whether American manufacturers with the best conditions for catching a cheater charge more.
items.finding: Moderately concentrated industries sit a few points above average

figures.alt: Price-cost ratio by concentration band
Margins against concentration for producer and consumer goods, 2022

items.paper: George J. Stigler, "A Theory of Oligopoly," Journal of Political Economy 72(1), February 1964, pp. 44–61 (DOI 10.1086/258853). Reprinted as chapter 5 of Stigler, The Organization of Industry (Homewood, Ill.: Richard D. Irwin, 1968), pp. 39–63.

items.title: Small Change for Large Prizes
items.dek: In 1967, Gordon Tullock argued that the money spent chasing tariffs and monopolies is a cost the standard measure leaves out. I went looking for that money in the tariff wars of 2018 and 2025.
items.finding: Lobbying about tariffs rose with the tariffs, and a step ahead of them

figures.alt: Lobbying reports mentioning tariffs and customs duties, 2008–2026

items.paper: Gordon Tullock, "The Welfare Costs of Tariffs, Monopolies, and Theft," Western Economic Journal 5(3), June 1967, pp. 224–232.

items.title: Bidding for the Bus
items.dek: In 1968, Harold Demsetz asked why a utility that can only have one supplier needs a regulator, when the right to be that supplier could be put up for auction. I asked again using the bus and paratransit routes American transit agencies put out to bid.
items.finding: Contracted service costs about a fifth less inside the same agency

figures.alt: In-house vs contracted cost per hour, 2025
The gap by year, and cost per hour around a switch

items.paper: Harold Demsetz, "Why Regulate Utilities?" Journal of Law and Economics 11(1), April 1968, pp. 55–65.

items.title: How Long a Patent Should Last
items.dek: In 1969, William Nordhaus worked out how many years an inventor should keep a monopoly before everyone else gets the idea for free. With Medicare's records of 95 brand-name pills going generic, I worked it out again.
items.finding: Nordhaus's table still comes out of his formula

figures.alt: Price and pills around generic entry
Optimal life as a function of x
Effective exclusivity

items.paper: William D. Nordhaus, Invention, Growth, and Welfare: A Theoretical Treatment of Technological Change, MIT Press, 1969 (MIT Monographs in Economics 10). The optimal-patent-life analysis reviewed here is the version circulated as William D. Nordhaus, "The Optimal Life of a Patent," Cowles Foundation Discussion Paper No. 241, Yale University, November 27, 1967 (38 pages).

items.title: Licensed to Cut Hair
items.dek: In 1971, George Stigler argued that regulation is bought by the people it regulates, and tested the idea on truck weight limits and state licensing laws. I reran his numbers and asked the licensing question again with 2024 data.
items.finding: Stigler's trucking regression reproduces from his own appendix

figures.alt: Rail haul and truck weight limits, 1932–33
License share against earnings, 2024

items.paper: George J. Stigler, "The Theory of Economic Regulation," Bell Journal of Economics and Management Science 2(1), Spring 1971, pp. 3–21.

items.title: Can You Monopolize Something That Lasts?
items.dek: In 1972, Ronald Coase argued that a company selling something durable ends up competing with itself. I tested the idea on twenty years of American manufacturing data.
items.finding: Concentration pays for goods that get used up, not for goods that last

figures.alt: Concentration and margins by product type
Comparing industries with each other and with themselves

items.title: Big Firms, Small Firms
items.dek: In 1973, Harold Demsetz asked whether the profits of concentrated industries came from collusion or from the superior efficiency of their largest firms. With the same IRS tax tables and the newest Census counts, I asked again.
items.finding: The largest firms no longer stand apart in concentrated industries

figures.alt: Returns by size and concentration, 1963 and 2012
Large-firm advantage against concentration, 2012
Payroll share, top four against the rest, 2022

items.paper: Harold Demsetz, "Industry Structure, Market Rivalry, and Public Policy," Journal of Law and Economics 16(1), April 1973, pp. 1–9 (JSTOR stable URL jstor.org/stable/724822).

items.title: Where the Rent Goes
items.dek: In 1975, Richard Posner argued that a monopoly costs society everything people spend trying to get one, and that monopolies created by government cost the most. Fifty years later, I checked his arithmetic and asked again, with sugar and real estate agents.
items.finding: Posner's printed costs subtract the triangle he meant to add

figures.alt: US and world raw sugar prices, 1980–2025
Agents per sale against home prices, 2023

items.paper: Richard A. Posner, "The Social Costs of Monopoly and Regulation," Journal of Political Economy 83(4), August 1975, pp. 807–827.

items.title: Bundling the Snack Aisle
items.dek: In 1976, William James Adams and Janet Yellen showed that a seller can earn more by selling two goods together than by selling them apart. I tested their idea on real bids for Snickers, Doritos and 58 other snacks.
items.finding: Selling two snacks as one pays in 60% of pairs, and only a little

figures.alt: Profit gain from bundling against the correlation of bids, 1,770 pairs
Share of pairs where pure bundling beats separate prices, by cost
Share of surplus captured as bundles grow, actual and shuffled bids

items.paper: William James Adams and Janet L. Yellen, "Commodity Bundling and the Burden of Monopoly," Quarterly Journal of Economics 90(3), August 1976, pp. 475–498. DOI 10.2307/1886045. Adams was at the University of Michigan and Yellen at Harvard University when it appeared.

items.title: The Empty Factory as a Warning
items.dek: In 1977 Michael Spence argued that a company could keep rivals out by building more factory than it needed, and in 1980 Avinash Dixit argued that it never would. I asked the Census Bureau's plant records which of them American manufacturing looks like today.
items.finding: Concentrated, capital-heavy industries run fuller, not emptier

figures.alt: Utilization against concentration, 2015-2019
Openings by new firms and incumbents against utilization two years earlier

items.paper: A. Michael Spence, "Entry, Capacity, Investment and Oligopolistic Pricing," Bell Journal of Economics 8(2), Autumn 1977, pp. 534–544 (DOI 10.2307/3003302). Read with its companion and correction, Avinash Dixit, "The Role of Investment in Entry-Deterrence," Economic Journal 90(357), March 1980, pp. 95–106 (DOI 10.2307/2231658).

items.title: When the Yen Fell, Prices Stayed Put
items.dek: In 1976 and 1977, Michael Spence, Avinash Dixit and Joseph Stiglitz built the model of monopolistic competition in which every seller keeps a fixed markup over its costs. I checked that markup against nearly twenty-three years of American import prices.
items.finding: Foreign sellers pass on about a fifth of a currency move

figures.alt: Pass-through by horizon
The yen and the dollar prices of goods from Japan

items.paper: Avinash K. Dixit and Joseph E. Stiglitz, "Monopolistic Competition and Optimum Product Diversity," American Economic Review 67(3), June 1977, pp. 297–308; read together with A. Michael Spence, "Product Selection, Fixed Costs, and Monopolistic Competition," Review of Economic Studies 43(2), June 1976, pp. 217–235.

items.title: The Octane Markup
items.dek: In 1978, Michael Mussa and Sherwin Rosen worked out how a seller should price a range of qualities to buyers it cannot tell apart. I asked whether the premium pump follows their rule.
items.finding: Premium carries a bigger margin than regular in 96% of months

figures.alt: Retail and wholesale premium spreads, 1995 to 2026
Ratio of retail to wholesale premium spreads, and premium's share of gallons and new models

items.paper: Michael Mussa and Sherwin Rosen, "Monopoly and Product Quality," Journal of Economic Theory 18(2), August 1978, pp. 301–317. DOI 10.1016/0022-0531(78)90085-6.

items.title: The Patient Gamer
items.dek: In 1979, Nancy Stokey proved that a seller who can hold to a price gains nothing by cutting it. I checked her prediction against the price histories of 143 games on Steam.
items.finding: Most list prices hold for a year, and many hold for good

figures.alt: Price paths after release
Launch share against publisher record

items.paper: Nancy L. Stokey, "Intertemporal Price Discrimination," Quarterly Journal of Economics 93(3), August 1979, pp. 355–371 (DOI 10.2307/1883163). Companion: Nancy L. Stokey, "Rational Expectations and Durable Goods Pricing," Bell Journal of Economics 12(1), Spring 1981, pp. 112–128.

items.title: What a Kilowatt-Hour Costs
items.dek: In 1979, Martin Loeb and Wesley Magat showed how a regulator who cannot see a utility's books could still get it to charge the true cost of one more unit of power. I measured how far 2025's electric rates sit from that price.
items.finding: Nearly every utility charges households far more than a kilowatt-hour costs

figures.alt: Residential prices against marginal cost by hub
Lerner index by class within each utility

items.paper: Martin Loeb and Wesley A. Magat, "A Decentralized Method for Utility Regulation," Journal of Law and Economics 22(2), October 1979, pp. 399–404, DOI 10.1086/466949. Read alongside its companion, Ingo Vogelsang and Jörg Finsinger, "A Regulatory Adjustment Process for Optimal Pricing by Multiproduct Monopoly Firms," Bell Journal of Economics 10(1), 1979, pp. 157–171.

items.title: What Netflix Charges the World
items.dek: In 1981, Richard Schmalensee asked when a seller who charges different customers different prices leaves the world better off. I asked again, using what Netflix and Disney+ charge around the world.
items.finding: With straight-line demand, one Netflix price would leave subscribers unchanged and the world $2 billion better off

figures.alt: Netflix 2024 regional demand curves and the single price
How the answer depends on the shape of demand

items.paper: Schmalensee, Richard. 1981. "Output and Welfare Implications of Monopolistic Third-Degree Price Discrimination." American Economic Review 71(1): 242–247. Circulated earlier as MIT Sloan School of Management Working Paper 1095-80, January 1980.

items.title: A Reputation for Fighting
items.dek: In 1982, Paul Milgrom and John Roberts, and separately David Kreps and Robert Wilson, showed why a company might rationally fight its first rivals at a loss to scare off the rest. I asked whether America's big airlines fight low-fare entrants, and whether fighting keeps the next one away.
items.finding: Incumbents cut fares by about 6% and kept their passengers

figures.alt: Incumbent fare and passengers around entry

items.paper: Paul Milgrom and John Roberts, "Predation, Reputation, and Entry Deterrence," Journal of Economic Theory 27(2), August 1982, pp. 280–312. Companion paper: David M. Kreps and Robert Wilson, "Reputation and Imperfect Information," Journal of Economic Theory 27(2), August 1982, pp. 253–279.

items.title: Reading Market Power off a Pack of Cigarettes
items.dek: In 1982, Timothy Bresnahan showed when an economist can tell a cartel from a competitive market without ever seeing its costs. I asked the question again of fifty years of American cigarette prices.
items.finding: The same pass-through gives opposite answers

figures.alt: Three estimates of cigarette conduct
Net-of-tax price and rolling conduct estimates

items.paper: Bresnahan, Timothy F. 1982. "The Oligopoly Solution Concept Is Identified." Economics Letters 10(1–2): 87–92. Companion survey named in the reading list: Bresnahan, T. F. 1989. "Empirical Studies of Industries with Market Power." In Handbook of Industrial Organization, Vol. 2, ch. 17. North-Holland.

items.title: Rent or Sell
items.dek: In 1982, Jeremy Bulow asked why a company that makes something durable would rather rent it out than sell it. Using the tax returns of every American manufacturer, I asked again.
items.finding: Renting lives almost entirely in durable final goods

figures.alt: Rent share and concentration across 63 manufacturing industries
Giants and everyone else, by industry, 2013

items.title: The Airline Waiting at the Gate
items.dek: In 1982 William Baumol argued that the threat of entry alone could hold a monopoly's prices to cost, and he pointed to the airlines. I asked his question again with eleven years of US airline tickets.
items.finding: The airlines flying a route set its price

figures.alt: 2024 fares by actual and potential competition
Incumbent fares after the Southwest threat

items.paper: William J. Baumol, "Contestable Markets: An Uprising in the Theory of Industry Structure," American Economic Review 72(1), March 1982, pp. 1–15 (the author's presidential address to the American Economic Association). Companion book: W. J. Baumol, J. C. Panzar and R. D. Willig, Contestable Markets and the Theory of Industry Structure, Harcourt Brace Jovanovich, 1982.

items.title: The Fare Cut Before Southwest
items.dek: In 1982 Paul Milgrom and John Roberts asked why a dominant firm would cut its price for a rival that has not arrived yet, and whether the cut keeps the rival out. I asked again with eleven years of airline tickets.
items.finding: Incumbents cut fares about 5% when Southwest arrives at both ends

figures.alt: Incumbent fares on threatened routes, by whether Southwest later came
Incumbent fares after each airline lands at both ends of a route

items.paper: Paul Milgrom and John Roberts, "Limit Pricing and Entry under Incomplete Information: An Equilibrium Analysis," Econometrica 50(2), March 1982, pp. 443–459. Manuscript received March 1980, revised December 1980.

items.title: Who Keeps the Savings
items.dek: In 1982, David Baron and Roger Myerson worked out how to regulate a monopoly whose costs the regulator cannot see. I asked whether America's electric utilities are paid the way their theory says they should be.
items.finding: Low-cost utilities earn more, by a little

figures.alt: Earned return on equity against wires-and-billing cost per customer
Revenue and net income responses to a $1 change in each cost

items.paper: Baron, David P., and Roger B. Myerson. 1982. "Regulating a Monopolist with Unknown Costs." Econometrica 50(4): 911–930. Earlier version: Northwestern University CMS-EMS Discussion Paper 412, 1979.

items.title: How Long Prices Stick
items.dek: In 1983 Guillermo Calvo asked what inflation looks like when sellers change their prices only now and then, at random moments. I put his answer to sixty years of American prices.
items.finding: Fitted to inflation, Calvo's model says prices last five years

figures.alt: Share of prices not yet changed, aggregate Calvo estimate vs. CPI micro frequencies
Estimated vs. Calvo-predicted Phillips-curve slopes by CPI category
Quarter of peak inflation by CPI category vs. months between price changes

items.paper: Guillermo A. Calvo, "Staggered Prices in a Utility-Maximizing Framework," Journal of Monetary Economics 12(3), September 1983, pp. 383–398. doi:10.1016/0304-3932(83)90060-0.

items.title: The Make Offer Button
items.dek: In 1983, John Riley and Richard Zeckhauser proved that a seller who can commit should name a price and refuse to haggle. I asked 88 million eBay listings whether holding firm pays.
items.finding: Sellers who committed to a firm floor earned more

figures.alt: Same catalogued product, different floors
Revenue after the first offer, by response

items.paper: John Riley and Richard Zeckhauser, "Optimal Selling Strategies: When to Haggle, When to Hold Firm," Quarterly Journal of Economics 98(2), 1983, pp. 267–289.

items.title: When the Big Chains Back a Higher Minimum Wage
items.dek: In 1983, Steven Salop and David Scheffman showed how a dominant firm can profit by raising its rivals' costs instead of cutting its prices. I asked whether rising minimum wages do that for America's largest restaurant and retail chains.
items.finding: A higher minimum wage cost big restaurant chains at least as much as their small rivals

figures.alt: Added payroll per 10% higher minimum wage, small vs. large firms
Change in large firms' share of jobs against the rise in the minimum wage
Restaurant prices against the rise in the minimum wage, 27 metro areas

items.paper: Steven C. Salop and David T. Scheffman, "Raising Rivals' Costs," American Economic Review 73(2), Papers and Proceedings, May 1983, pp. 267–271.

items.title: The Last Kilowatt-Hour
items.dek: In 1984, Eric Maskin and John Riley worked out how a seller should price when it cannot tell big buyers from small ones, and pointed to the electric bill as proof. I checked 2026's electricity tariffs to see whether the proof still holds.
items.finding: Bigger buyers pay less per kilowatt-hour

figures.alt: Bill per kWh by household use
Bill per kWh and price of the next kWh
Price above wholesale, by class

items.paper: Eric Maskin and John Riley, "Monopoly with Incomplete Information," RAND Journal of Economics 15(2), Summer 1984, pp. 171–196. Author affiliations as printed: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (Maskin) and University of California, Los Angeles (Riley).

items.title: The Trigger Price
items.dek: In 1984 Edward Green and Robert Porter explained why a cartel that never cheats still has price wars. I tested their theory on fifty years of OPEC oil.
items.finding: Oil prices do switch regimes, and the low regime is nearly a third cheaper

figures.alt: Oil prices and Saudi plus UAE output, with the low-price regime shaded
Each low-price episode, price change against Saudi plus UAE output change

items.paper: Edward J. Green and Robert H. Porter, "Noncooperative Collusion under Imperfect Price Information," Econometrica 52(1), January 1984, pp. 87–100.

items.title: Paying Hospitals What They Spend
items.dek: In 1985 Andrei Shleifer showed that paying each firm the costs of its peers, rather than its own, makes it cut costs. Medicare pays most hospitals by that rule and over a thousand small rural ones by their own costs, so I asked whether the difference shows.
items.finding: Cost-reimbursed hospitals cost more per patient because they are smaller

figures.alt: Cost per adjusted discharge against volume, and the adjusted gap by year
Event study around conversion to critical access status

items.paper: Andrei Shleifer, "A Theory of Yardstick Competition," RAND Journal of Economics 16(3), Autumn 1985, pp. 319–327.

items.title: The Supercharger Moat
items.dek: In 1985, Michael Katz and Carl Shapiro asked whether the biggest network wins because it is the biggest, and whether it will ever agree to share. I asked again, with every new battery-electric car sold in Washington State and every public fast charger in the country.
items.finding: Teslas did not cluster where the Superchargers were

figures.alt: Tesla share of new cars and of fast-charging ports in Washington
Who opened their chargers

items.paper: Michael L. Katz and Carl Shapiro, "Network Externalities, Competition, and Compatibility," American Economic Review 75(3), June 1985, pp. 424–440.

items.title: Bargaining Against Yourself
items.dek: In 1986, Faruk Gul, Hugo Sonnenschein and Robert Wilson proved that a seller who cannot promise to hold firm ends up bargaining against his own future offers. I asked what their theory predicts about how long American strikes last, and checked it against 1,984 of them.

figures.alt: Opening price and time to sale in Example 1
Share of strikes still running after day 3, with the two fitted models
Strikes still running, first contract against existing relationships

items.paper: Faruk Gul, Hugo Sonnenschein and Robert Wilson, "Foundations of Dynamic Monopoly and the Coase Conjecture," Journal of Economic Theory 39(1), 1986, pp. 155–190.

items.title: What Cement Prices Do in a Boom
items.dek: In 1986, Julio Rotemberg and Garth Saloner argued that firms who quietly agree not to compete are most likely to break ranks when business is best. I rebuilt their evidence and ran it again on data through 2023.
items.finding: Cement prices were countercyclical before 1982

figures.alt: Cement prices against GNP growth, before and after 1982
Share of industries where the real wage rises with employment, by concentration

items.paper: Rotemberg, Julio J., and Garth Saloner. 1986. "A Supergame-Theoretic Model of Price Wars during Booms." American Economic Review 76(3): 390–407. Circulated as "A Supergame-Theoretic Model of Business Cycles and Price Wars During Booms," NBER Working Paper 1412, August 1984.

items.title: Who Pays the Overrun
items.dek: In 1986, Jean-Jacques Laffont and Jean Tirole worked out how a government should pay a firm whose costs it can see but whose effort it cannot. I asked whether the American transit agencies that pay contractors in the two textbook ways get different costs.
items.finding: Cost reimbursement does not raise the cost of an hour

figures.alt: Cost per hour by payment basis, 2025
Real cost per hour by payment basis, 2017 to 2025

items.paper: Jean-Jacques Laffont and Jean Tirole, "Using Cost Observation to Regulate Firms," Journal of Political Economy 94(3), June 1986, pp. 614–641, DOI 10.1086/261392.

items.title: The Price of Leaving
items.dek: In 1987, Philippe Aghion and Patrick Bolton asked whether a contract that a customer signs willingly can keep out a cheaper competitor. I asked again, using every plan on the state of Texas's electricity comparison site.
items.finding: Texas fees shut out four in five cheaper offers

figures.alt: Share of cheaper offers shut out over the life of a contract
Cancellation fees against lost profit

items.paper: Philippe Aghion and Patrick Bolton, "Contracts as a Barrier to Entry," American Economic Review 77(3), June 1987, pp. 388–401.

items.title: Why Prices Sit Still
items.dek: In 1987 Olivier Blanchard and Nobuhiro Kiyotaki argued that market power is what lets small costs of changing a price keep prices frozen. I checked whether the producers with the most market power really do change their prices least.
items.finding: The raw slope matches the theory

items.title: What the Next Unit Costs
items.dek: In 1988, Robert Hall argued that American industry sells its goods for far more than it costs to make one more of them. I asked the question again with factory data running to 2016 and industry accounts running to 2025.
items.finding: Hall's pattern is still there, and larger by his yardstick

items.title: The Browser That Came With the Phone
items.dek: In 1990, Michael Whinston showed how a company that controls one product can tie a second one to it and push that market's rivals out. I asked how far the tie reaches in the browsers people use today.
items.finding: A tied browser takes most of its own phone

figures.alt: Browser share vs. platform share by country
The platform owner's browser on its own platform
Choice screens, EU vs. comparison countries

items.paper: Michael D. Whinston, "Tying, Foreclosure, and Exclusion," American Economic Review 80(4), September 1990, pp. 837–859. Circulated earlier as NBER Working Paper No. 2995, June 1989.

items.title: The Price of New Ideas
items.dek: In 1990 Paul Romer argued that growth comes from new designs, and that the monopoly markup on each design is what pays for the research behind it. I checked both halves against American data.
items.finding: Research effort rose sevenfold while productivity growth halved

Price-cost margin against R&D intensity, 36 manufacturing industries

items.title: Who Owns the Kilns
items.dek: In 1990, Oliver Hart and Jean Tirole worked out when a supplier buys its customers in order to shut their rivals out, and they pointed to cement as a case. I went back to the cement industry with data from 2002 to 2023 to see how the theory holds up.
items.finding: Every regional cement market is concentrated by the paper's own yardstick

Williamson (pp. 280–283) and a general discussion (pp. 283–284) follow, with references on pp. 285–286.

items.title: How Big a Town Needs to Be
items.dek: In 1991, Timothy Bresnahan and Peter Reiss counted the doctors, dentists, druggists, plumbers and tire dealers in 202 isolated towns, mostly western county seats, to measure how much each new seller toughens competition. I counted them again in 445 towns.
items.finding: A small town now needs far more people to keep its first shop

Entry thresholds in 2000 and 2016

items.title: Locking Up the Customers
items.dek: In 1991, Eric Rasmusen, Mark Ramseyer and John Wiley showed how a dominant company could shut out a rival by paying its customers almost nothing. I asked how much of an American market that would take today.
items.finding: A single plant is a sliver of almost every American market

Fewest customers at which one-at-a-time offers exclude

items.title: The Advertising Floor
items.dek: In 1991, John Sutton argued that industries built on advertising stay concentrated however large their market grows, while commodity industries fragment. I asked again with the 2022 Economic Census and the filings of 42 food and drink companies.
items.finding: No advertising-heavy food industry has a top four below 30%

Average top 4 share by group, 2002 to 2022

items.title: The Bill Follows the Cost
items.dek: In 1991, Jean-Jacques Laffont and Jean Tirole showed that a regulator who might be captured should give the firm it oversees weak incentives to cut costs. I measured how weak those incentives are for American electric utilities, and whether they are weaker where utility commissioners run for office.
items.finding: American utilities bear about a fifth of their non-fuel costs

items.title: Who Climbs the Ladder
items.dek: In 1991, Gene Grossman and Elhanan Helpman described economic growth as a ladder that challengers climb and leaders fall off. Using company filings from 2012 to 2024, I checked who is doing the climbing.
items.finding: Leaders in research-heavy industries are not replaced any faster

items.title: How Long a Lead Lasts
items.dek: In 1992, Philippe Aghion and Peter Howitt modeled economic growth as a chain of innovations, each one ending the monopoly of the one before, so that more research should mean shorter reigns at the top. I checked that against fourteen years of revenue rankings for every company that files annual reports with the SEC.
items.finding: Industry leaders fall about once a decade, with or without research

Research effort and productivity growth

items.title: The Markup in a Boom
items.dek: In 1992, Julio Rotemberg and Michael Woodford argued that American firms shave their markups when demand is strong, and that this is why a surge in government spending raises both jobs and wages. I rebuilt their evidence and asked again with data through 2025.
items.finding: Today's data reproduce the 1999 chapter's signs, and some of its numbers

Responses to military spending

items.title: Fixed Price or Cost-Plus
items.dek: In 1993, Jean-Jacques Laffont and Jean Tirole worked out how a government should pay a contractor whose costs it can see but whose effort it cannot. I asked whether the contracts NASA and the Department of Energy actually sign behave the way their theory says.

items.title: The Taylor Rule Fit Its Own Era
items.dek: John B. Taylor (1993) asked whether a two-term formula could describe how the Federal Reserve sets interest rates. I rebuilt his rule from the data he had in 1992 and tested it against sixty years of revised data, the Fed staff's own real-time forecasts, an external instrument, and an estimated New Keynesian model.
items.finding: On the data Taylor had, the rule fits to within 0.40 points

items.title: How Much Gets Passed On
items.dek: In 1995 Miles Kimball asked how much of a cost change a firm passes on when its customers flee a high price faster than they flock to a low one, and how much that slows inflation. I asked again at the US border, with fourteen years of import prices.

items.title: The Pioneer's Share
items.dek: In 1995, Jerry Green and Suzanne Scotchmer asked how the profit from an invention is divided when someone else builds the next one on top of it. I asked again, with 1.2 million American patents and the stock market's valuation of each.

items.dek: In 1995, Steven Berry, James Levinsohn and Ariel Pakes asked how much of a new car's price is markup when no two models are alike. I rebuilt their estimate from the 1971 to 1990 car data as it is distributed today, then checked the piece of their model that makes luxury cars different on what Washington drivers paid for plug-in cars from 2017 to 2025.

items.title: The Price of Admission

items.title: Buying Patents and Giving Them Away

items.title: The Competitive Benchmark
items.dek: In 2002, Severin Borenstein, James Bushnell and Frank Wolak measured how far California's wholesale electricity prices ran above competitive levels in the 2000 crisis. I rebuilt their benchmark for California and Texas, 2019 to 2025.

items.title: More Car for the Money
items.dek: In 2024 Paul Grieco, Charles Murry and Ali Yurukoglu asked whether American carmakers gained or lost market power between 1980 and 2018. I asked again with public data, and followed the question through the chip shortage.
items.finding: Concentration fell by as much as the paper says

items.paper: Paul L. E. Grieco, Charles Murry and Ali Yurukoglu, "The Evolution of Market Power in the US Automobile Industry," Quarterly Journal of Economics 139(2), 2024, pp. 1201–1253. First circulated as NBER Working Paper 29013 (July 2021).

items.title: Minnesota Climate Project
items.dek: An original county-year study of what repeated wet years do to housing, farming and local economies across Minnesota, built from NOAA weather records and public county data.
items.finding: Repeated wet years are most clearly associated with fewer permit units, lower construction GDP, and lower corn and soybean yields.

items.title: Sectoral Inflation & Tariff Dynamics
items.dek: Python and Julia scripts that pull disaggregated CPI from FRED and chart sector-by-sector inflation against the dates major tariffs took effect, in 2018–2019 and again in 2025–2026.
